stories.title: U-M Climate Week returns with expanded events, engagement
stories.summary: The University of Michigan will host its second annual Climate Week from Sept. 26-Oct. 3, bringing together students, faculty, staff and community partners for a week of events focused on climate action, research, education and engagement. This year’s Climate Week has grown to include programming across the Ann Arbor, Dearborn and Flint campuses and Michigan Medicine, with events organized by schools, colleges, units and community partners.

The week-long initiative, launched in 2025, aims to connect climate-related work across the university and with external communities, offering opportunities for service and hands-on activities.

stories.summary: The University of Michigan has paused its pilot program that would have replaced letter grades with 'pass' or 'no credit' for some freshmen in the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts. stories.title: U-M Regent Joins Ypsilanti Data Center Protest
stories.summary: University of Michigan Regent Paul Brown joined a protest against the university's planned $1.25-billion computing center on the Huron River in Ypsilanti Township. Brown criticized the university for insufficient community engagement and called for a halt to the project, which faces ongoing opposition from residents and officials. The protest follows more than a year of community resistance to the facility, with the university maintaining it is a high-performance research computing center.

stories.summary: University of Michigan student caregivers are facing challenges due to gaps in childcare services, impacting their academic and personal lives. The article highlights the struggles of balancing caregiving responsibilities with university demands, particularly among graduate students and those supported by organizations like GEO. Negotiations around student protections and resources remain ongoing.

stories.summary: A University of Michigan study outlines design principles for future nitrate remediation strategies, which could help address ecosystem damage caused by excessive algae growth. Dr. Nathaniel Szymczak discusses the research during an interview with WEMU's Caroline MacGregor, noting the work may take decades to implement but represents a critical step forward.

stories.summary: The University of Michigan will host a second town hall on Oct. 1, 2026, regarding its partnership with Los Alamos National Laboratory to build a data center in Ypsilanti Township. The event, held at Ypsilanti Marriott at Eagle Crest, will include a guided discussion and Q&A, with livestreaming available due to full in-person registration. stories.title: U.P. prison smuggling plot uncovered after monthslong investigation
stories.summary: A Muskegon woman and several inmates are suspected of participating in a drug smuggling plot at the Baraga Correctional Facility in Michigan's western Upper Peninsula. The Michigan Department of Corrections (MDOC) and Michigan State Police (MSP) uncovered the scheme after finding drugs left in a prison restroom in January 2026. The investigation revealed a sophisticated operation involving multiple inmates and associates, with contraband including K2, high-potency THC wax, and suboxone strips. MDOC Director Heidi E. Washington emphasized the dangers of contraband entering facilities and the collaboration with law enforcement to hold suspects accountable.

photo.alt: U.P. prison smuggling plot uncovered after monthslong investigation

stories.title: U.P. school cancels classes after morning break-in. What happened
stories.summary: Classes at an Upper Peninsula school were canceled on Oct. 1, 2026, after a 24-year-old DeTour man broke into DeTour Area Schools early in the morning. The suspect was arrested and charged with breaking and entering and malicious destruction of property. School officials canceled classes to assess damage and make repairs, with classes tentatively resuming on Oct. 2.

photo.alt: Portrait of Dan Basso

stories.title: U.P. wildfires 20-25% contained after weather shift aids crews
stories.summary: Cooler temperatures and higher humidity helped firefighters gain 20-25% containment on two Upper Peninsula wildfires, prompting officials to lift an evacuation order for some residents. The Ridge Fire (450 acres, 20% contained) in Marquette County and Craig Lake Fire (400 acres, 25% contained) in Baraga County remain challenging due to remote, rugged terrain. An air quality alert persists across multiple counties due to wildfire smoke.

This decision preserves the current election process for the upcoming November election but leaves open the possibility of future changes. A new poll shows declining voter confidence in Michigan's election system, with 74.4% of likely voters believing it is fair and accurate, down from 79.4% in 2025.

stories.title: UAW members recall tense encounters with Mike Rogers during his time in Congress
stories.summary: As Mike Rogers campaigns for a U.S. Senate seat, UAW members describe strained interactions with him during his 2001-2015 congressional tenure. Tensions arose during meetings where UAW members lobbied against policies like trickle-down economics and NAFTA, which Rogers supported. The UAW and other unions have endorsed Rogers' Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed, while business groups back Rogers.

stories.title: UAW tries to reassert political power in Michigan as the union faces internal divisions
stories.summary: The United Auto Workers union is working to reassert its political influence in Michigan ahead of the 2026 midterms, but faces internal divisions among members over party alignment and trust in leadership. Retired workers and union members express mixed support for Democratic and Republican candidates, while past corruption scandals and closed-door negotiations have eroded confidence in the union's leadership.

stories.title: Uber driver killed, passenger ejected in Oak Park crash
stories.summary: An Uber driver was killed and a passenger ejected in a crash in Oak Park. Later, a second driver with a blood alcohol level three times the legal limit struck an unoccupied patrol car during the traffic diversion. The driver was arrested for operating under the influence, and bodycam footage was shared to raise awareness about drunk driving dangers.

photo.alt: Uber driver killed, passenger ejected in Oak Park crash

stories.summary: Ukrainian officials confirmed resuming attacks on Russian oil refineries following a temporary ceasefire, escalating tensions in the conflict.

stories.title: UM Detroit Center’s Block x Block series: Open dialogue on issues of concern, centering Detroiters’ lived experiences
stories.summary: The University of Michigan Detroit Center (UMDC) launches the Block x Block series, a monthly public engagement initiative featuring community leaders, UM faculty, and Detroit residents discussing systemic issues like poverty, housing, and immigration. The series emphasizes face-to-face dialogue to center lived experiences and foster university-community collaboration. The first event on September 17 will focus on immigration with speakers from the Detroit Hispanic Development Corporation and UM-Dearborn.

stories.title: UM regent donates 11 acres, funds retreat north of Ann Arbor campus
stories.summary: University of Michigan Regent Mark Bernstein and his wife Rachel Bendit have donated 11 acres of land and $500,000 in funding to create the Bernstein Leadership Retreat and Joy Farm near Ann Arbor. The property, located at 4981 Gleaner Hall Road, will serve as a retreat space for students, faculty, and staff with programming supported by the donation. The gift was approved during the October 15 Board of Regents meeting held on the Flint campus.

photo.alt: The Bernstein Leadership Retreat and Joy Farm will provide a wooded gathering space just 15 minutes from campus, with programming funded by the donor family.

stories.title: UMich awards Wallenberg Medal to Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef
stories.summary: The University of Michigan awarded the 31st annual Wallenberg Medal to Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef at Rackham Auditorium. Jozef, co-founder of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, delivered a lecture on immigration crises and human rights, addressing the termination of Haitian immigrants' protected status and ongoing humanitarian challenges in Haiti. Over 300 attendees, including students and community members, heard her call for collective action to protect immigrant communities.

photo.alt: Guerline Jozef receiving the Wallenberg Medal at the University of Michigan.

stories.title: UMich awards Wallenberg Medal to Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef
stories.summary: The University of Michigan awarded the Wallenberg Medal to Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef, the 31st recipient, who highlighted the termination of Haitian immigrants' temporary protected status by the Trump administration and the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Haiti. Jozef emphasized migration as a human right and called for collective action to address Haitian immigration as a humanity issue rather than a political one.

photo.alt: Guerline Jozef speaks at a podium.

stories.title: UMich Board of Regents discusses recent construction projects and satellite campuses
stories.summary: The University of Michigan Board of Regents convened to discuss recent construction projects and developments related to satellite campuses. The meeting focused on infrastructure advancements and strategic campus expansions.

stories.title: UMich Board of Regents discusses recent construction projects and satellite campuses
stories.summary: The University of Michigan’s Board of Regents met at the Flint campus to discuss construction projects and satellite campuses. President Domenico Grasso addressed attendees, highlighting U-M Flint’s 70th anniversary. The meeting was part of the Board’s penultimate session of the calendar year.

stories.title: UMich computer science no longer requires specialized application as demand steadies
stories.summary: The University of Michigan has eliminated the specialized application process for computer science majors as demand for the program has stabilized. Previously, students had to select their college (Engineering or LSA) and declare interest via a checkbox or transfer application. stories.title: Urban, rural hospitals closing at similar rates, study finds
stories.summary: A new study published in JAMA found urban and rural hospitals are closing at similar rates, with shuttered hospitals more likely to serve high-poverty areas with limited transportation. Researchers analyzed 2010-2025 data showing 432 closures and 216 openings, while the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid cuts and rural health grants are reshaping healthcare access.
entities: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

stories.title: US reviving shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing electricity demand, power data centers
stories.summary: The United States is attempting to restart three shuttered nuclear plants—Palisades in Michigan, Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania, and Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa—to meet rising energy demand, particularly for data centers. The Department of Energy is providing up to $4.4 billion in loans for these projects, which aim to restore 2.25 gigawatts of electricity. Two plants have contracts with Big Tech companies for carbon-free energy, while experts debate the safety, cost, and necessity of these restarts.

stories.summary: Detroit is upgrading hundreds of bus stops with new shelters and benches to improve the public transportation experience. stories.title: Warren double homicide from 1981 reopened, but evidence was destroyed
stories.summary: Warren police have reopened a 1981 double homicide case involving Cheryl Kemp and Lisa Schwartzkopf, but physical evidence from the crime was destroyed or released decades ago. Families of the victims are seeking closure as detectives use modern DNA technology to re-examine the cold case. The original evidence included bullets, clothing, and biological samples, with some items sent to the Michigan State Police lab before being lost in an inventory error.

Police state drugs and alcohol were not factors, and the daughter is cooperating with investigators.

stories.title: We spoke to 6 Metro Detroit doctors about rising e-bike injuries in kids — here's what they said

Emergency department visits for e-bike-related injuries among patients under 18 rose 7.5-fold between 2023 and May 2026, with over a third sustaining head or neck injuries. stories.title: 'We were blindsided': Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan responds to AG complaint

The lawsuit accuses BCBSM of operating an illegal monopoly and conspiring with other insurers to fix prices, inflating costs for consumers. stories.title: ‘What environmental racism looks like’: Protest targets University of Michigan computing center

stories.title: When do leaves change colors in Michigan? Where leaves are turning now
stories.summary: Michigan's diverse tree varieties each display unique fall color patterns, according to Michigan State University Extension. In the Upper Peninsula and northern Lower Peninsula, maple trees turn orange and red, while quaking aspen and larch trees produce yellow leaves. Southern Michigan features red oaks with subtle red tones, white oak group trees with yellow or dusty red leaves, and sassafras with yellow to deep red foliage. Hickories and larch varieties like tamarack also contribute to the fall palette with yellow hues.

photo.alt: When do leaves change colors in Michigan? Where leaves are turning now

stories.title: When do the Orionids peak?
stories.summary: The Orionids meteor shower will be active from Oct. 2 to Nov. 7, peaking overnight on Oct. 21-22, according to NASA. Known for its fast, bright meteors, the shower produces about 10 to 20 meteors per hour, traveling at 41 miles per second and leaving glowing trails. The meteors appear to originate from the constellation Orion, though it is not their actual source.

stories.title: When does daylight saving time end in 2026?
stories.summary: Unless Congress acts, daylight saving time is scheduled to end at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, when clocks move back one hour to 1 a.m. The shift provides an extra hour of sleep but results in earlier sunsets during winter. The change is unlikely to affect Halloween, as it occurs after the holiday on Oct. 31.

stories.title: Why are judicial races in Michigan separated by incumbency?
stories.summary: Michigan's 1982 law separates incumbent and non-incumbent judicial candidates on ballots, creating distinct sections for each. The change, lobbied for by sitting judges, aimed to reduce campaign fundraising pressures and ethical dilemmas. Critics argue it insulates incumbents from competition, while proponents claim it allows judges to focus on their work and gives newcomers a fairer shot at judicial positions. The law remains in effect for 2026 elections, with 16 incumbent judges running in Wayne County's 3rd Circuit Court.

The article highlights tensions between clean energy transitions, rising utility costs, data center expansion, and the Line 5 pipeline controversy. These issues reflect broader debates about balancing economic development with environmental stewardship in the Great Lakes state.

stories.title: Ypsi officials and activists prepare for climate emergency
stories.summary: Ypsilanti officials and community organizers are expanding efforts to address climate-related emergencies like extreme heat and wildfire smoke. Initiatives include opening cooling centers, distributing masks and water, and improving communication networks to reach vulnerable populations. The county is developing air quality response plans and collaborating with community organizations to enhance preparedness.

stories.title: Ypsilanti-area ICE operation draws crowd before individual’s release, sheriff says
stories.summary: Federal immigration agents attempted to detain an individual in Ypsilanti Township, prompting a crowd to gather. The person was later released after showing a green card, and ICE agents left the scene after deputies de-escalated the situation. Washtenaw County Sheriff Alyshia Dyer emphasized the sheriff’s office does not participate in immigration enforcement.

stories.title: Ypsilanti City Council fails to pass resolution opposing police budget ballot proposal
stories.summary: A resolution opposing Proposal B on the Ypsilanti November ballot, which would require a public vote to increase the city’s police budget, failed to secure the required majority during a 3-2 council vote. Council members expressed divided opinions, with some arguing the proposal could harm police morale and others questioning the need for voter approval given existing budget processes. Mayor Nicole Brown and Councilmember Me’Chelle King were absent at a conference.

photo.alt: Ypsilanti City Council meeting on October 6, 2026

stories.title: Ypsilanti City Council to be asked to oppose police budget ballot proposal
stories.summary: Ypsilanti City Council member Patrick McLean is urging his colleagues to officially oppose city ballot Proposal B, which would require a public vote to increase the police budget. McLean argues the charter amendment could harm the city’s budget, while Council member Amber Fellows believes voters should decide. The resolution will be introduced at Tuesday’s City Council meeting.

stories.title: Ypsilanti officials consider data center ordinance proposal
stories.summary: The City of Ypsilanti is evaluating a proposed ordinance to update zoning laws for data centers, presented by City Planner Josh Burns on Sept. 15. The proposal includes categorizing data centers by size, setting energy and water consumption limits, and establishing noise and environmental regulations. Councilors discussed concerns about noise, health impacts, and water usage, with the city planning to enforce standards for setbacks, lot coverage, and cooling systems.

stories.title: Ypsilanti police chief reports crime uptick, staffing challenges
stories.summary: Ypsilanti Police Chief Timothy Anderson reported a 30% increase in calls for service and significant rises in violent crimes like assaults and homicides during a City Council meeting. He highlighted staffing challenges with six officer vacancies and high turnover, attributing retention issues to competitive job markets and community tensions. The city faces an upcoming November ballot proposal that would require voter approval for annual police budget increases, sparking debate over policing accountability and funding.

photo.alt: Ypsilanti police chief reports crime uptick, staffing challenges

stories.title: Ypsilanti Police Report Staffing Challenges and Crime Uptick
stories.summary: Ypsilanti Police Chief Timothy Anderson reported 27 officers with six vacancies at a recent City Council meeting, citing competitive job markets and anti-police narratives as retention challenges. A November ballot proposal could require voter approval for annual police budget increases, with supporters calling it democratic accountability and opponents warning of defunding risks. The department faces ongoing scrutiny after a controversial 30-hour barricade incident involving a man with a mental health crisis.

stories.title: Ypsilanti Symphony Orchestra opens 2026-27 season Oct. 4
stories.summary: The Ypsilanti Symphony Orchestra (YSO) will open its 2026-27 season titled 'Playing Favorites' on Oct. 4, 2026, with a concert featuring familiar classical pieces and new works. Music director Adam C. Riccinto emphasized blending recognizable music with fresh compositions throughout the season, including holiday pops and community-focused events. Concerts will take place at Lincoln High School and Riverside Park, with ticket prices ranging from $7-15.

stories.title: Ypsilanti Township residents push back on University of Michigan data center project
